recognize: someone the prompt doesn't already have, or several people, named by the part's own words: "young man", "nurse", "my friend", "elderly African man", "couple", "three friends". Their noun is one of those words. Two parts with the same words are two different people.

Words that name only something about a person, or about someone the prompt already has in its own words or as another part ("1girl, ⟨hairstyle⟩", "a woman with ⟨hair color⟩ hair", "1boy, ⟨outfit⟩, ⟨expression⟩", "a knight in ⟨armor⟩", "a ⟨1: girl⟩ with a ⟨2: shy smile⟩"): their expression, pose, face, body or clothes, are never a person, even when that is all the part is about: that person is already in the prompt. They are a "list" when a list below covers them, else "free".
reader.heading: For a person:
reader.category: "" for a person: "elderly African man", "young woman", "chef" and "couple" keep all their words.
reader.one: A person named by name (a character, a real person: "Sherlock Holmes"), someone the prompt names elsewhere, or people the words settle exactly ("identical twin boys") are "one": every image shows that same someone. "old man", "nurse", "young woman", "couple", "three friends" and a person the prompt only describes ("a tall woman in a red coat") are "kind".

questions.ask: what they are, in one word from their words ("man", "nurse", "friend").
questions.required: part {n}: a person's noun is one of their own words, and "{value}" is not among the words "{words}". Words that name only something about a person, or about someone the prompt already has, are a "list" when a list covers them, else "free"

questions.ask: "feminine" or "masculine" when their words or the notes say which, else "".

how the prompt or the notes say this person looks, read anywhere in the prompt, not only in their own words: for each person detail below that is stated of them, the words that state it, copied exactly ("elderly African man": {"age": "elderly", "descent": "African"}; "⟨1: woman⟩, long wavy red hair, pale skin, slim": {"hair": "long", "hair_texture": "wavy", "hair_color": "red", "skin": "pale skin", "build": "slim"}). Each detail on its own: hair is only how long it is, hair_texture only its texture, hair_color only its color, hairstyle only how it is worn (a braid, a ponytail, bangs, a bun); words that state one of them leave the others unstated, and words that state two of them are split between them ("braided platinum hair": {"hair_color": "platinum", "hairstyle": "braided"}), never given whole to one. skin is only its tone or color, build only the shape and size of the body, eyes only their color, age only how old they are; words about anything else (body hair, fangs, sweat, a scar, makeup) state no detail. Only what is said of this very person, never of someone else in the prompt; nothing guessed, nothing implied by who they are, their role or the style of the picture. {} when nothing is said, which is common.
questions.note: The prompt already says how this person looks: {looks}. Every variant keeps all of that exactly as the prompt says it, never changing or contradicting any of it, and leaves it unsaid; the rest of how they look still varies from variant to variant, including what the prompt leaves open about their hair (its texture or style when only its length is said).

questions.needs_message: part {n}: a person needs details to vary, some of age, descent, build, hair; words that name something about a person or about someone the prompt already has (their expression, pose, face, body or clothes) are not a person: they are a "list" when a list covers them, else "free"
questions.ask: the details that change from image to image, from the person details below. They are the fixed things about the person: their age, within what the words say ("young man" stays young, "elderly African man" stays elderly and of African descent), their descent, build, hair and the like. Most often: age, descent, build, hair, hair_texture and hair_color, with facial_hair for a masculine person. hairstyle only when the prompt or a note asks for it to change. Choose what this picture shows of them: a small figure in a wide scene shows age, build and hair, not eyes; a close portrait adds eyes. You need not include every detail, but leave one out only for a reason. Facial hair only for a masculine person.
more: Leave out expression unless the prompt or a note asks for it to change. Leave out pose and accessories: they are not part of the person.

questions.ask: when another numbered part is what they wear, or some of it, its number: 2 in "⟨1: woman⟩ in a ⟨2: kimono⟩" or "⟨1: man⟩ in ⟨2: pajamas⟩"; else 0.

when another numbered part is their face, or features of it, its number: 2 in "⟨1: woman⟩ with ⟨2: face⟩" or "⟨1: old man⟩ with ⟨2: weathered features⟩"; else 0. A part that is only their expression ("⟨2: shy smile⟩") is not their face: 0.
questions.note: Another part of the prompt is this person's face: describe none of it (no face shape, eyes, brows, nose, lips, jaw, cheeks, skin marks or lines). Their expression may still show.

questions.ask: the words of the prompt or a note that say what they wear, copied exactly ("in a red raincoat", "in a nurse's uniform"); "" when nothing says so, which is most prompts.

options.note: None of what they wear shows in this picture, and maybe little of their body: write no clothes, shoes, hat or jewelry, and no build or height when only their face shows. Still say who they are as the seed line gives them (their gender, age and heritage), then how what shows of them looks (their face, hair, skin, expression), in words of your own: the prompt's words after the part already say what is in frame, so never repeat them.

questions.ask: "hidden" when, read in the whole prompt, none of what they wear would show: something covers them (bedcovers, bathwater or foam, a towel wrapped around them, water up to the head, a wall or a counter with only their face above it) or the framing is so close that only their face or part of it is in frame; "" when any of their clothes would show, which is most prompts (a portrait, a waist-up shot, someone sitting on a bed, someone behind a bar).

"implied" when who they are and where they are say what they wear, as working dress, a uniform or religious dress does (a nurse, a chef, a firefighter, a welder, a monk, a nun, a cowboy, a soldier, a farmer at work); "" when it doesn't ("a woman", "a man at a cafe", "a student"), which is most prompts.

questions.invalid: part {n}: outfit "{value}" is not one of the lists
questions.ask: their clothes change too, unless clothes has words, clothes_part names a part or shows is "hidden". Give the id of the outfit list below that suits the scene, or "written" if none does, as for most dress that is implied (no list holds a firefighter's turnout gear or a nun's habit); "" only when clothes has words, clothes_part is not 0 or shows is "hidden".

questions.none: "" when it doesn't say, which is most prompts.
questions.invalid: part {n}: place "{value}" is not a country's name: give only the country the picture is set in, by its plain common name in English ("Vietnam", "Japan", "Morocco"; England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland or Hawaii as themselves), or "" when the prompt doesn't say

questions.ask: who the part's words name, read in the whole prompt

options.note: The marked words name a couple. Each variant describes both partners briefly, as two people who belong together, in one phrase that keeps the marked words where they read naturally ("young Ugandan couple, the man in a crisp white shirt, the woman with her braids pinned up"), never tacked on at the end ("..., couple"). Each variant contains the marked words. Say who they are as the seed line says, through the two of them. Their ages are about the age given and close to each other, unless the prompt says otherwise. A look idea may suit one of them or both. 12 to 35 words beyond the marked words.

options.text: people related to each other: "family", "mother and daughter", "grandparents", "siblings"
options.note: The marked words name a family or other related people. Each variant names its members, two or more ("a father in his fifties with his grown daughter and her husband"), each with an age that suits their role, and gives them the heritage they share and a family likeness; a look idea may suit one of them or several. Unless the scene is one for adults only, a family has children among its members, at ages that suit them ("a mother in her thirties with her two boys, six and nine"). 12 to 35 words beyond the marked words.

options.text: people who aren't related: "three friends", "coworkers", "a crowd", "a band"
options.note: The marked words name several people who aren't related. Each variant gives each of them a few words of their own, one by one ("two coworkers, a tall woman in a gray suit and a stocky man with a shaved head"), never one description for all of them, so they read as different people (heritage, gender, age and look as the prompt allows), adults unless the prompt's words make one a child, with as many people as the words say. 12 to 35 words beyond the marked words.

questions.ask: what sort of being they are, read in the whole prompt

options.text: a real-world human, who has a heritage and the look of one

any other sort of being, to whom a real people's heritage doesn't apply: a fantasy being, a robot, an alien, a demon, an animal character, a toy, a statue, a figure in a style with no real people's looks

require_one.message: part {n}: a person's clothes change unless the prompt says what they wear: when another part is what they wear, give its number as "clothes_part"; when the prompt's own words say, copy them into "clothes"; else give an outfit list's id, or "written" when none suits

jewelry, glasses and other things they wear

typical.text: how someone like them is typically dressed here, from any headwear they typically wear down to their feet
without: hair and how it is worn

examples: "a ⟦young woman⟧ in a kitchen" (keep "young woman") -> "freckled young woman with a short black bob"

"a ⟦dominant young woman⟧ in a living room", three variants with their seed lines ("Tunisian", develop: face and expression / "Korean", develop: styling and grooming and jewelry, glasses and other things they wear / "Peruvian", develop: build and what they wear, ideas: "tall") -> "dominant young woman of Tunisian heritage, strong dark brows and a sharp jaw, a cool, level stare that dares the camera to look away", "dominant young woman, Korean, hair slicked straight back, a dark lip, heavy silver rings stacked on every finger", "tall, broad-shouldered dominant young woman, Peruvian, in a fitted black blazer worn over bare skin, sleeves pushed up"
rules: A person variant says only who they are and how they look: their age, heritage, build, face, hair, expression, grooming and what they wear. Never what they are doing, how they stand, sit or hold themselves, a gesture, anything they hold or carry, or anything else in the scene (other people, animals, furniture, the place): the rest of the prompt owns those. When the prompt's own words give them an action or a thing ("a man reading"), leave it to the prompt and add none of your own.

A person: 12 to 25 words beyond the marked words. Write each variant as an authored take on who this is, leaning into the marked words themselves: for "dominant young woman", how her dominance shows in her face, expression and styling, and in what she wears when the prompt leaves that open. Each variant develops the aspects its seed line names, so the set differs in far more than hair. No shared template: vary how each variant is phrased and where things fall in it (the marked words first in some, after a detail in others: "broad-shouldered Peruvian dominant young woman in a fitted blazer"; the descent before the words, after them, or as "of Tunisian heritage"), and weave its seeds in where they read naturally, never as a list or a prefix. Never describe what another part of the prompt owns (a clothing part elsewhere owns the clothes).
seed_rules: a quoted descent: give the person that heritage's look (the look given with it in brackets, when there is one), and write that exact word or words into the variant where it reads naturally. If the marked words name several people, it is the heritage they share, unless the line gives one for each. When it can't be true in this prompt (a figure who isn't of that people, such as a creature or a stylized character, or a setting or the user's words that settle who they are), leave it out and list it under "rejected", copied exactly. A descent marked (must appear) is always written in.
gender: write the person as that, with those exact words in the variant ("a woman", "a young man"), woven in naturally; the marked words still stay.

who: who the couple are. Say it through the two of them, in the variant's own words ("the man in a linen shirt, the woman with her hair pinned up"; "two women in their thirties"), never as a label repeated at the end.

develop: the aspects of the person this variant describes in particular; others lightly or not at all. Hair is one aspect among many, not a must. "How someone like them is typically dressed here, from any headwear they typically wear down to their feet": beside who they are (their heritage, gender and age as the line gives them), what most people like them wear at work or in this place and time, from what is on their head down to their feet, working dress included, as a photograph of a real one would show them (a fisherman's sou'wester, oilskins and boots; a nurse's scrubs and a lanyard around the neck), never a tool or anything in their hands. When people like them typically cover their head here, with a hat, helmet, cap, veil or scarf, put it on their head and leave their hair unsaid.

age: about how old the person looks; work it in before their words ("a 34-year-old chef") or say it another natural way ("a chef in her forties"), never as a number tacked on at the end. When the prompt already says their age, write it no second time.
writer.one: This part names one particular someone: every variant is that same person or those same people, as the marked words and the prompt give them, with their own look, sex and age; a named character or real person looks as they are known to look. Never change who they are, add anyone to them, or make them a child unless the words do.
